concept.name: Type II error
concept.definition: Failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false - a false negative. Its probability is denoted beta, and 1 - beta is the power of the test.
concept.intuition: It is missing a real edge: the strategy genuinely works, but your sample was too small or noisy for the test to detect it.
concept.mechanics: Beta depends on the true effect size, the sample size, the significance level, and the noise level: larger effects and larger samples shrink beta, while a stricter alpha (to avoid Type I errors) increases it. The two error types trade off against each other for a fixed design.
concept.formula: beta = P(do not reject H0 | H0 is false); power = 1 - beta.
concept.failure_modes: Small samples are the main culprit: with 20 trades, only a very large edge is detectable, so most genuinely positive strategies fail to reach significance. Heteroskedastic or autocorrelated returns inflate the effective noise and raise beta beyond the textbook value.
concept.misconceptions: Failing to reject H0 is not evidence that H0 is true - a high-beta test simply could not see the effect. Also, alpha and beta are not complements (alpha + beta != 1); they are error rates under different states of the world.
concept.example: A strategy with a true 0.1% mean daily edge tested on 50 days will usually yield p > 0.05 - a Type II error - because the standard error swamps the small true effect at that sample size.
